opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what we believe physical AI needs to succeed. For language models, the whole community benefited from openness: papers, open weights, shared datasets, people building on each other's work. Physical AI is at an earlier stage. Robotics, autonomous vehicles, and embodied agents all need a model that understands how the world works, how objects move and interact, and what happens when you take an action. That's a very hard problem, and no single company is going to solve it alone.

So with Cosmos, our view has always been that we want to be a platform the community can build on. Releasing only weights isn't quite enough. If researchers and developers really want to adapt the model to their own robot, their own factory, or their own driving domain, they need to know how it was built: how we curated the data, how we designed the tokenizer, the architecture choices, the training recipe, the post-training. When you document things at the level where someone could reproduce it, you lower the barrier for everyone. A university lab can try a new idea without starting from zero. A startup can fine-tune for its own use case and trust what's underneath.

There's also a scientific reason. Reproducibility is how a field makes progress. If we claim a model has good physical understanding, others should be able to check that, find where it fails, and improve it. Honestly, a lot of the most valuable feedback we get comes from people pushing the model in directions we didn't anticipate.

And from NVIDIA's perspective, it aligns well with what we do. We build the computing infrastructure. If the physical AI ecosystem grows and more people are training and deploying world models, that's good for everyone, including us. So openness isn't charity. It's our belief that the fastest way to get physical AI working in the real world is to let many more people participate in building it.

r001.rationale: The response advocates openness but does not say that many frontier AI labs withhold technical details when publishing papers.

r002.rationale: It says the goal is to make Cosmos a platform others can build on and that sharing how it was built lets them reproduce and adapt it.

r003.rationale: The response supports reproducibility, but does not express a lack of concern about others reproducing Cosmos exactly.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The short answer is that I don't think a world foundation model should be something only one company can build. Physical AI — robots, autonomous vehicles, anything that has to act in the real world — is going to touch a lot of industries, and most of those industries don't have the resources to train a model like this from scratch. If we keep the recipe closed, we slow the whole field down, and honestly we slow ourselves down too.

Let me unpack that a bit. When we started Cosmos, we were trying to solve a data problem. Robotics doesn't have an internet's worth of training data the way language models do. You can't scrape a trillion robot trajectories off the web. So the idea was to build a model that understands how the physical world behaves — how objects move, how light works, how a hand interacts with a cup — and use that as a foundation that others can fine-tune for their specific robot, their specific factory, their specific car. That only makes sense if people can actually get at it and adapt it.

With Cosmos 3 we went further than just releasing weights. We tried to document the data curation pipeline, the tokenizer design, the training schedule, the places where we got it wrong before we got it right. Part of that is a research culture thing — I come from a background where you publish, people check your work, and the field moves. Part of it is practical. If a lab in Shenzhen or a startup in Munich reproduces our result and finds a better curation strategy, we learn from that. If they can't reproduce it, they can't trust it, and they certainly won't build on it.

There's also a safety argument that I think gets lost. People sometimes assume openness and safety are in tension. For world models, I'd say the opposite. The failure modes of a physics simulator that hallucinates — an object passing through a table, a car that doesn't decelerate the way it should — those are much easier to find when thousands of people are poking at the model instead of a few dozen inside one company. We want those bugs found before the model is sitting inside a robot on a factory floor.

And then, if I'm being candid about the business side: NVIDIA sells the compute. The more people building physical AI, the better for us. We don't need to own the model to benefit from the ecosystem. That alignment is a big reason I can push for openness internally and not get much pushback.

So it's a mix. Scientific conviction, practical necessity, and incentives that happen to point the same direction. I feel fortunate about that.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention other frontier AI labs publishing papers while withholding technical details.

r002.rationale: It says Cosmos is meant to be adapted for specific robots, factories, and cars, and that documenting its pipeline lets others reproduce and build on the work.

r003.rationale: It welcomes others reproducing the result and says they can learn from others’ improvements, conveying no concern about others reproducing Cosmos.

That also makes the research more credible—you shouldn’t have to take our word for it. My hope is that making Cosmos 3 openly available lowers the barrier for people to contribute and helps the whole field move forward.
